brief_problem: How many pizzas should we order for the party?

runs.text: Programming is solving a problem and then explaining the solution to a computer so clearly that it cannot get it wrong.
The problem
Year five is organising the end-of-year party at the school kiosk.
23 people
are coming. Each one eats
3 slices
of pizza, and each pizza has
8 slices
How many pizzas do we have to order?
Try it
Before reading on, solve it with pencil and paper. You do not need to know how to program: you need to think.
23 people times 3 slices is 69 slices. With 8 pizzas you have 64 slices: 5 are missing. You have to order
9 pizzas
If you answered 8, five people go hungry. If you answered 8.6, nobody sells six tenths of a pizza. Both answers come from doing the sum right and not looking at the question.
What you just solved is a
problem
: a situation with values you know (23 people, 3 slices, 8 per pizza) and a question that has no answer yet. Programming always starts like this: with a problem, not with a computer.
The PseudoLearn cycle
To solve any problem you will always follow the same five steps. Together they make
the PseudoLearn cycle
. At first we guide you through each one; with time you will do them without thinking.

blocks.description: Five steps in a circle: Understand, Plan, Write, Test and Improve, joined by solid arrows. A red dashed arrow goes back from Test to Plan when something failed, and another dashed arrow goes from Improve to Understand, towards the next problem.

caption.text: The solid arrows are the usual path. If something fails when you test it, you do not start from scratch: you go back to planning.

rows.text: What am I given, what am I asked, and can I solve it by hand?
Which steps do I follow, and in what order?
How do I tell the computer?
Does the computer answer the same as I did by hand?
Can I explain it in one sentence? What if the request changes?

runs.text: Now go through the five steps with the pizza problem.
Understand
Understanding means separating what you know from what you are asked, and checking that you could solve it without a computer.

entries.text: 23 people, 3 slices per person, 8 slices per pizza.
how many pizzas. Notice a detail in the question: pizzas are ordered

runs.text: The best way to understand a problem is to solve concrete cases with pencil and paper. Each one is a
worked example
. It helps twice: now, to discover how to solve it, and in step 4, to know what the computer must answer. Always do at least two.
The second example teaches something: when the division is exact, you must not order an extra pizza.
Plan
Look at what you did in the examples and write it as steps, in your own words:

entries.text: Multiply the people by the slices each one eats.
Divide that result by the slices in one pizza.
If the result has decimals, round up.

runs.text: That is already the solution. What is left is telling it to the computer.
Write
A
program
is a list of orders written for a computer. Each order is an
instruction
. The computer reads them from top to bottom, one at a time, and does exactly what each one says: no more, no less, and not what you meant.

blocks.description: On the left, a program with three Write instructions; on the right, the output. Each step highlights one instruction and its line appears in the output: first Hola, then 5 and finally 2 + 3.

caption.text: Each step runs a single instruction and adds one line to the output, always from top to bottom.

The second computes 2 + 3 and shows the result.
The third shows the text as it is, because it is between quotes.

blocks.title: Party, first attempt

runs.text: The computer did exactly what you asked: divide. It does not know that pizzas are ordered whole, because nobody told it. Step 3 of the plan is missing.
PseudoLearn comes with ready-made calculations.
is a
built-in function
: it receives a number between brackets and returns the whole number above it if the number has decimals, or the same number if it has none.

Porciones que hacen falta: 69

runs.text: The first line of the body does step 1 of the plan; the second does steps 2 and 3 together. If you want to know exactly how each thing you used is written, it is in the Specification. You do not need to read it now: it is the place to look up a doubt.
Test
A program showing a number does not mean the number is right. Testing is comparing what the computer answers with your worked examples. For the second example, change 23 to 8 and run it again:

blocks.title: Party with 8 people

runs.text: The 8-people example was the important one: it is the case where a hurried solution orders one pizza too many. The exercises in this lesson teach you to look for those cases on purpose.
Improve
Explain it in one sentence. If you cannot, you do not fully understand it yet:
The program works out how many whole pizzas are enough for everybody to eat their slices
What if the request changes? Tomorrow they confirm
30 people
who eat
2 slices

each. To adapt it you have to find the 23 and the 3 inside the instructions and change them on every line where they appear. In a program of a hundred lines, missing one would be easy to do, and the program would give a wrong result without warning.
What you learned

points.text: A problem has known values and a question; before programming, you read the question carefully.
A worked example is a case solved with pencil and paper; it helps you discover the solution and check it.
A program is a list of instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom, exactly as they are written.
The output is what the program shows; what goes between quotes is shown as it is and the rest is computed.
, receives a value and returns another.
The PseudoLearn cycle has five steps: understand, plan, write, test and improve.

runs.text: Practise
No exercise tells you what to write. It gives you a problem, and the cycle is yours.

runs.text: Before running, the engine reads the text, checks that it is well written and turns it into smaller orders the machine knows how to do. That journey is told, with figures, in the Specification.
